flashcards.q: Why is yield-based fixture teardown more robust than manual setUp/tearDown?
flashcards.a: Teardown code lives lexically right after the setup it corresponds to in the same function, making it harder to forget updating it when setup changes. pytest also guarantees the post-yield code runs even if the test raises an exception.

flashcards.q: Fixture scope tradeoff: function vs session?
flashcards.a: function (default): fresh per test, no cross-test state leakage risk, pays setup cost every time. session: created once for the whole run, essential for expensive setup, but risks order-dependent flaky tests if any test mutates shared state.

flashcards.q: What's the real value of @pytest.mark.parametrize beyond avoiding duplication?
flashcards.a: It turns test cases into a data table -- adding a new edge case becomes a one-line addition rather than writing a new test function, which materially lowers the friction of adding regression tests and means more edge cases actually get covered over time.

flashcards.q: What is a genuine 'property' in property-based testing, vs an example-based check?
flashcards.a: A statement true across the ENTIRE input space (round-trip: decode(encode(x))==x; invariant: max(lst) is always in lst), not one expected output for one input. Not every function has a useful property -- arbitrary business-rule lookups often don't, and recognizing that is part of the skill.

flashcards.q: Why does Hypothesis's shrinking matter practically?
flashcards.a: Without shrinking, a failure reports whatever large random input triggered it first. Shrinking searches for the simplest input still reproducing the failure, converging on a small, human-readable counterexample -- turning 'a bug somewhere in a huge blob' into an actionable minimal repro.

flashcards.q: What does mutation testing measure that line coverage cannot?
flashcards.a: Whether tests would actually catch a real bug, not just whether a line executed. It injects mechanical mutations (operator swaps, boundary shifts) and reruns tests -- a SURVIVING mutant is concrete proof no assertion verifies that specific logic, even on a 100%-covered line.

flashcards.q: Does a high mutation score guarantee bug-free code?
flashcards.a: No -- it only proves sensitivity to the tool's specific catalog of mechanical mutations (operator swaps, negations, constant shifts). It says nothing about a fundamentally wrong algorithm or a bug that doesn't correspond to any mutation in that catalog.

flashcards.q: Why is mutation testing rarely run on every commit?
flashcards.a: Cost scales as (mutable code locations) x (one full test-suite run per mutant) -- for a nontrivial module this can take hours, far slower than linting or a single test run. Typically scoped to critical modules or changed code, run periodically rather than continuously.

flashcards.q: Why is a differential property (new impl vs reference impl) a good fit for testing a performance optimization?
flashcards.a: The goal of an optimization is 'same output, faster execution' -- there's no new expected output beyond what the slower reference already produces, so asserting optimized(x)==reference(x) across many generated inputs gives far broader correctness confidence than a handful of hand-picked comparisons.
